lessons.title: Closings in Colorado
lessons.body:
## Who is responsible for a Colorado closing?

In most Colorado transactions a title company (the [[closing company]]) actually runs the closing: it prepares the settlement figures, collects funds, records documents, and disburses money. That does **not** take the broker off the hook. The Commission's rule on closing responsibility puts it this way:

- A broker who has a brokerage relationship with a buyer or seller (as an agent or transaction-broker) is **responsible for the proper closing** of the transaction.
- That broker must make sure the consumer receives an **accurate, complete and detailed [[closing statement]] that is signed by the broker**.
- The broker must **review the closing documents** and **attend the closing or be reasonably available**. If the broker can't, another broker designated by the brokerage firm may step in — and that substitute broker then shares responsibility for the accuracy, completeness and delivery of the signed statement.
- Closing statements and other closing documents go to the **brokerage firm** right after closing for the transaction file, and the employing broker's supervisory duties still apply.
- A broker who prepares and closes the documents personally is responsible for their accuracy and completeness.

The license law backs this up: failing to give the buyer and the seller a closing statement is a ground for discipline (C.R.S. 12-10-217(1)(j)), as is failing to account for or remit other people's money within a reasonable time.

> **Exam tip:** "The title company prepared it, so it isn't my problem" is always the wrong answer. Hiring a closing company delegates the *work*, not the broker's *responsibility* to check the statement and see that the parties receive it.

## Closing instructions

The Commission-approved **[[Closing Instructions]]** form is the engagement agreement between the parties and the closing company. Key points:

- It is signed by the **buyer, the seller and the closing company**. The brokers are not parties to it, although they receive copies of required documents and statements.
- The closing company agrees to prepare closing statements, deliver and record documents, and disburse funds (including commissions) according to the contract.
- If party instructions conflict with the contract, the buyer and seller must sign an amendment (Agreement to Amend/Extend Contract).
- The closing company may not release signed documents or things of value until **[[good funds]]** are received and disbursed.
- The contract has a checkbox showing whether Closing Instructions are signed with the contract or later.

## Good funds

Colorado's good funds law (C.R.S. 38-35-125) says a closing or settlement provider may not disburse until the funds have been received and are **available for immediate withdrawal** — wire transfers and certified, cashier's or teller's checks qualify. A personal check for a large down payment does not. The provider may advance a small amount (up to $500) for incidental items such as tax certificates and recording fees. The Commission's closing rule repeats this: a broker or firm may not disburse, or authorize disbursement, before the funds are good.

## Closing statement vs. Closing Disclosure

| | Closing statement (settlement statement) | [[Closing Disclosure]] |
|---|---|---|
| Source | Commission-approved form or closing company's statement | Federal TRID rule (CFPB) |
| Required by | Colorado license law and Commission rule | Federal law for most consumer mortgage loans |
| Covers | Every transaction, cash or financed | Loan terms and costs for the borrower |
| Broker duty | Ensure it is accurate, complete, signed by the broker and delivered | Not the broker's form, but review for consistency |

A cash sale has no Closing Disclosure, but it still needs a closing statement. The Commission's closing statement uses **[[debits]]** and **[[credits]]** for each party, a line for each common charge (documentary fee, recording, title premiums, taxes, HOA items, rents and security deposits, Colorado withholding, FIRPTA), and signature lines for the buyer, seller and broker.

## Delivering documents

Colorado brokers must give **copies (duplicates) of every document they prepare** to the consumers involved when the document is prepared, and the parties must get a signed copy of the listing contract and the contract of sale. After closing, the firm keeps the closing statement and closing documents in its transaction file.

## Recording

Colorado is a **[[race-notice]]** state (C.R.S. 38-35-109): an unrecorded deed or other instrument isn't valid against a later buyer who records first without notice of it. That is why the closing company records the deed (and the buyer's deed of trust) with the **[[County clerk and recorder|county clerk and recorder]]** right away. Two items usually travel with the deed:

- **[[Documentary fee]]** — a state fee collected by the clerk and recorder when the deed is recorded: **one cent per $100 of consideration** (a "major fraction" of $100 counts as a full $100), with no fee when consideration is $500 or less (C.R.S. 39-13-102). On a $400,000 sale that's $40. The contract doesn't assign it to a party, so check the closing statement and local practice; don't confuse it with *local* transfer taxes, which some home-rule cities charge and which the contract lets the parties allocate.
- **[[Real property transfer declaration]]** (form TD-1000) — filed with the deed so the assessor learns the sale price. The clerk sends it to the assessor; it is not a public record. If the grantee doesn't file it after notice, the assessor can charge a penalty.

## Title insurance customs in Colorado

The contract (section 8) handles title:

- If neither box is checked, the **seller selects the title company and pays for the [[owner's title insurance policy]]**, furnishing a title commitment for the purchase price.
- The parties may instead check that the buyer selects the title company and pays for the owner's policy.
- The buyer's lender requires a **[[lender's policy]]**, which the buyer normally pays for as a loan cost.
- **[[Owner's extended coverage]] (OEC)** removes the standard exceptions (such as unrecorded mechanics' liens and matters a survey would show). The contract says whether OEC will be provided and who pays the extra premium; the title company may require a new survey or improvement location certificate.
- The title company typically gets a **[[Certificate of taxes due|certificate of taxes due]]** from the county treasurer, and the contract says who pays for it.

> **Exam tip:** In Colorado, a seller paying for the buyer's owner's policy is the contract default — the reverse of many other states. Remember "seller selects, seller pays" unless the contract says otherwise.

## Withholding at closing

The closing company also handles two kinds of tax withholding from the seller's proceeds when required: federal **[[FIRPTA]]** withholding if the seller is a foreign person, and Colorado **[[Colorado nonresident withholding|nonresident withholding]]** (covered in the taxes lesson). The contract authorizes the closing company to withhold and remit.

## Quick checklist for the broker

1. Review the Closing Instructions and make sure they match the contract.
2. Send the closing company accurate figures and any amendments in writing.
3. Review the draft closing statement line by line against the contract (price, earnest money, concessions, prorations, who pays which fee).
4. Attend closing or be reasonably available; sign the closing statement.
5. Get the signed statement and documents to your brokerage firm right after closing.

lessons.title: Prorations and settlement math
lessons.body:
## The language of settlement

Every [[closing statement]] is a set of **[[debits]]** (what a party owes or is charged) and **[[credits]]** (what a party receives or is given credit for).

Think of each party's column as a **running tab**:

- A **debit** is something the party owes. For the buyer it raises the cash they must bring; for the seller it lowers the check they take home.
- A **credit** is something in the party's favor. For the buyer it lowers the cash they must bring; for the seller it raises their check.

So for every line, the question is simply **"who owes whom?"** The party who owes is debited; the party who is owed is credited. A good way to keep the common items straight:

| Item | Buyer | Seller |
|---|---|---|
| Purchase price | Debit | Credit |
| Earnest money | Credit | — (already in the price) |
| New loan proceeds | Credit | — |
| Payoff of seller's loan | — | Debit |
| Seller concessions | Credit | Debit |
| Unpaid current-year property taxes (seller's share) | Credit | Debit |
| HOA dues prepaid by seller | Debit | Credit |
| Rent collected by seller for days buyer will own | Credit | Debit |
| Tenant security deposits | Credit | Debit |
| Brokerage commission paid by seller | — | Debit |

The rule of thumb: when one party has **paid ahead** for something the other party will use, the payer gets a **[[credit]]** and the other party a **[[debit]]**. When an expense has **built up but hasn't been paid** (accrued), the party who owes it is **[[Debit|debited]]** and the party who will end up paying it is **[[Credit|credited]]**.

## Which column? Three questions

When an item isn't obvious, ask these in order.

**1. Does money move between the buyer and the seller, or between one party and an outsider?**

- **Between the buyer and the seller** (price, concessions, prorations, deposits handed over, an assumed loan): it's a **double entry**. The same amount is a debit to one party and a credit to the other.
- **Between one party and an outsider** (a lender, the county, the title company, a brokerage): it's a **single entry** in that party's column only. Paying an outsider is a debit (payoff, commission, title charges); money coming in for the buyer is a credit (earnest money already paid, the new loan).

**2. For a double entry that isn't a proration: who owes whom?** The buyer owes the price (buyer debit, seller credit). The seller owes a concession or the tenants' deposits (seller debit, buyer credit). An assumed loan is part of the price the buyer pays by taking over the seller's debt (seller debit, buyer credit).

**3. For a proration: has the bill been paid already, or will it be paid later?**

| The bill was... | Example | Entry | For whose days? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paid ahead by the seller | HOA dues, propane or heating oil in the tank | **Buyer debit, seller credit** | The buyer's days (the buyer reimburses the seller) |
| Collected ahead by the seller | Rent for the month of closing | **Seller debit, buyer credit** | The buyer's days (the seller hands over the buyer's share) |
| Not paid yet; the buyer will pay it later ([[paid in arrears]]) | Colorado property taxes, interest on an assumed loan, a water bill paid after the period | **Seller debit, buyer credit** | The seller's days (the seller pays the buyer for time the seller used) |

In short: **paid in advance → buyer debit, seller credit. Paid in arrears → seller debit, buyer credit.** Rent collected in advance is the one that looks backward: the seller already *received* the money, so the seller owes the buyer.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which column does a closing item go in?
  accDescr: Start with an item on the closing statement. If money moves between one party and an outsider such as a lender, the county, a title company or a brokerage, it is a single entry: a payment out is that party's debit, and money coming in for the buyer, such as earnest money or the new loan, is a buyer credit. If money moves between the buyer and the seller, it is a double entry. If it is not a proration, debit the party who owes it and credit the party who is owed. If it is a proration, ask whether the bill was paid ahead by the seller, collected ahead by the seller, or will be paid later. Paid ahead by the seller, such as HOA dues or fuel: buyer debit, seller credit for the buyer's days. Collected ahead by the seller, such as rent: seller debit, buyer credit for the buyer's days. Paid later, such as Colorado property taxes or interest on an assumed loan: seller debit, buyer credit for the seller's days.
  A["An item on the closing statement"] --> B{"Between buyer and seller, or with an outsider?"}
  B -- "With an outsider" --> C["Single entry, one column only"]
  C --> C1["Paying out: that party's debit"]
  C --> C2["Money in for the buyer: buyer credit"]
  B -- "Between buyer and seller" --> D{"Is it a proration?"}
  D -- "No" --> E["Double entry: debit who owes, credit who is owed"]
  D -- "Yes" --> F{"When is the bill paid?"}
  F -- "Seller paid ahead" --> G["Buyer debit, seller credit for the buyer's days"]
  F -- "Seller collected ahead" --> H["Seller debit, buyer credit for the buyer's days"]
  F -- "Paid later, in arrears" --> I["Seller debit, buyer credit for the seller's days"]
```

> **Check yourself:** on a correct statement, every double entry shows up **twice** (once in each party's column, same amount), and every single entry shows up **once**. If an item appears on both sides but the amounts differ, one of them is wrong.

## [[Prorations]] under the Colorado contract

The Commission's residential contract (section 16) prorates listed items **to the Closing Date** unless the parties agree otherwise:

- **[[General real estate taxes]]** for the year of closing, plus personal property taxes and special taxing district assessments.
- **Rents** — on rents actually received or accrued (the contract has a checkbox). The seller must transfer or credit **[[security deposits]]** for assigned leases and notify tenants in writing.
- **Other items** such as water and sewer, propane, and interest on a loan the buyer takes over.
- **[[Assessments|Association assessments]]** — regular assessments the seller paid in advance are credited to the seller; reserves the association holds for deferred maintenance are **not** credited to the seller unless the governing documents say so. The seller must ask for an association **[[status letter]]** at least 14 days before closing, and pays its fee.
- Prorations are **final** unless the parties agree otherwise in writing.

### Property taxes are paid in arrears

Colorado property taxes for a year become due on **January 1 of the following year** (C.R.S. 39-10-102). They can be paid in full by the end of April, or in two halves — the end of February and June 15. So at a closing in, say, June 2026, the 2026 taxes have not been billed yet. The seller owned the property for part of 2026 and the buyer will pay the whole 2026 bill next year — so the seller's share is a **debit to the seller and a credit to the buyer**.

Because the current year's bill isn't known yet, the contract sets a default basis: **the taxes for the calendar year immediately before closing**, using the most recent mill levy and the most recent assessed (actual) valuation — unless the parties check a different option. Any unpaid *prior-year* taxes are paid off by the seller in full as a debit.

> **Exam tip:** "[[Paid in arrears]]" taxes → **seller debit, buyer credit** for the seller's days. Don't credit the seller for taxes unless the problem says the current year was already paid.

## How to do a proration

1. Find the **daily (or monthly) rate**: annual amount ÷ 365 (or 360, or 12 months, as the question directs).
2. Count the **days** the seller owned or used the item in the period.
3. Multiply, then decide who is debited and who is credited.

Exam problems tell you which day-count method to use and who owns the day of closing. In the examples below, the year has 365 days and the **buyer owns the day of closing**, so the seller's days run through the day before closing.

### Example 1: Taxes in arrears

Last year's taxes were **$3,650**. Closing is **June 15** (not a leap year). Taxes for the current year are unpaid.

- Daily rate: $3,650 ÷ 365 = **$10.00**
- Seller's days: January 1 through June 14 = 31 + 28 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 14 = **165 days**
- Seller's share: 165 × $10 = **$1,650**
- Entry: **debit seller $1,650, credit buyer $1,650**

### Example 2: Rent collected in advance

A seller of a rental collected June's rent of **$1,800** on June 1. Closing is **June 15** in a 30-day month; the buyer owns the day of closing.

- Daily rent: $1,800 ÷ 30 = $60
- Buyer's days: June 15 through June 30 = **16 days**
- Buyer's share: 16 × $60 = **$960**
- Entry: **debit seller $960, credit buyer $960** (the seller collected money that belongs to the buyer)

If the tenant also paid a **$2,000 security deposit**, the seller transfers it: debit seller $2,000, credit buyer $2,000. A deposit is not prorated — it moves over in full.

### Example 3: HOA dues paid in advance

The seller paid the **$300** monthly HOA dues for June. Closing is June 15 (30-day month), buyer owns the closing day.

- Daily: $300 ÷ 30 = $10; buyer's days = 16
- Entry: **credit seller $160, debit buyer $160** (the seller prepaid days the buyer will enjoy)

### Example 4: Documentary fee

Sale price **$485,000**: $485,000 ÷ 100 = 4,850 units × $0.01 = **$48.50**.

## Putting a statement together

A $400,000 sale closing June 15. Buyer put down $10,000 earnest money and gets a new $320,000 loan. The seller owes $250,000 on an existing loan, pays a $20,000 commission and $1,500 for the owner's title policy. Use the tax and HOA figures from Examples 1 and 3, and assume a $150 seller-paid status letter fee and a $40 documentary fee charged to the buyer.

**Seller**

- Credits: price $400,000 + prepaid HOA $160 = **$400,160**
- Debits: payoff $250,000 + commission $20,000 + owner's policy $1,500 + tax proration $1,650 + status letter $150 = **$273,300**
- Net to seller: $400,160 − $273,300 = **$126,860**

**Buyer**

- Debits: price $400,000 + documentary fee $40 + HOA $160 = **$400,200**
- Credits: earnest money $10,000 + loan $320,000 + tax proration $1,650 = **$331,650**
- Cash due from buyer at closing: $400,200 − $331,650 = **$68,550** (before the buyer's own loan costs)

Notice the **tax proration appears on both statements** (debit seller, credit buyer), while the **[[loan payoff]]** and **[[Brokerage fee|commission]]** appear only on the seller's side and the **new loan** only on the buyer's side.

> **Exam tip:** Items that appear on **both** sides are prorations and transfers between the parties. Items that appear on only **one** side are paid to or received from a third party (lender, broker, title company, county).

## Common traps

- Earnest money is a **buyer credit**, never a seller debit — it's part of the price the seller is already credited with.
- The **buyer's new loan** is a buyer credit and doesn't appear on the seller's side.
- An **[[assumed loan]]** is a buyer credit and a seller debit.
- The **[[documentary fee]]** is based on the full consideration, not just the down payment.

lessons.title: Property management and landlord-tenant in Colorado
lessons.body:
## Property management needs a license

Under Colorado's license law (C.R.S. 12-10-201(6)), anyone who **rents or leases real estate for another for compensation**, or offers or lists property for rent, is acting as a real estate broker — including a person working as an employee of the owner for a salary or fee. So a property manager who leases and manages other people's property for pay must hold a Colorado broker's license and work under a brokerage firm.

The main exception is narrow: a **regularly salaried employee of the owner of an apartment building or condominium units who acts as the on-site manager**, and only for the customary duties of an on-site manager for that employer. An owner managing their own property also doesn't need a license.

## Trust accounting for rents and deposits (brief)

Money a property manager collects belongs to owners and tenants, so it goes into [[trust accounts]]:

- A firm that manages property must keep **separate trust accounts for rents and for security deposits** — at least one for each.
- Property management funds must be deposited within **five business days** after receipt (or after the lease is signed, if later). Other trust money, such as earnest money, has a shorter three-business-day deadline.
- No commingling: firm operating money stays out of trust accounts (except as rules allow), and earned fees are withdrawn promptly.
- Owners get regular accountings, generally within 30 days after month end unless the management agreement says otherwise.
- If the owner, rather than the firm, will hold the security deposits, the tenant must be told in writing who holds the deposit and how to get it back. When management changes firms, the tenant and owner must get a written account of the deposits.

## [[Security deposits]]

Colorado tightened its deposit rules over the last several years, most recently with HB25-1249, which took effect January 1, 2026. As of this writing:

| Rule | Colorado law |
|---|---|
| Maximum deposit | **Two months' rent** (C.R.S. 38-12-102.5, effective 2023) |
| Return deadline | **30 days** after the lease ends or the tenant surrenders the premises, whichever is later — unless the lease sets a longer time, **not more than 60 days** (C.R.S. 38-12-103; "one month" before 2026) |
| Deductions | Only for actual cause, in reasonable amounts; **never for normal wear and tear** or for damage that existed before the tenancy |
| Itemization | A **written statement listing the exact reasons** for anything withheld, delivered within the deadline; if the tenant asks in writing, the landlord must also provide supporting documents (photos, receipts, invoices) within 14 days |
| Missing the statement | The landlord **forfeits** the right to keep any part of the deposit |
| Wrongful retention | **Treble** (three times) the amount wrongfully withheld, plus attorney fees and costs; the tenant must give the landlord at least **7 days' notice** of the demand and intent to sue before filing, and the landlord has the burden to prove the withholding wasn't wrongful. Keeping 125% or more of actual damages is presumed unreasonable |

> **Exam tip:** "30 days, or up to 60 days if the lease says so" is the Colorado return rule (older materials say "one month"). A 14-day, 45-day or "within 10 days" answer is a distractor.

When a rental is **sold**, the landlord (or its agent) has 60 days to either transfer the deposits to the new owner and notify the tenants, or return them to the tenants less lawful deductions. That's why the closing statement moves deposits from seller to buyer. A 2026 law (SB26-054) also lifts the two-month cap, starting January 1, 2027, for deposits under a **[[post-closing occupancy agreement]]** in which a seller stays on briefly after closing.

## [[Warranty of habitability]]

Every Colorado residential lease carries an implied promise that the unit is **fit for human habitation** (C.R.S. 38-12-503). The tenant can't waive it. Basics:

- The tenant gives the landlord **written or electronic notice** of the problem (in the way the landlord usually communicates) and keeps proof.
- The landlord must **respond within 24 hours** after receiving notice.
- For a condition that **materially interferes with life, health or safety**, the landlord must start fixing it within **24 hours**; for other conditions that make the unit uninhabitable, within **96 hours** (if the tenant gave permission to enter).
- For a condition that materially interferes with life, health or safety, the landlord must, if the tenant asks, provide a comparable unit or hotel room at no cost (the tenant still owes rent).
- Mold tied to dampness has its own containment steps within 96 hours.
- Conditions caused by the tenant, household members or guests are **not** a breach by the landlord.
- The tenant also has duties: keep the unit reasonably clean and safe, use the facilities reasonably, dispose of trash properly, and promptly tell the landlord about problems.

## Eviction basics (these change often)

Eviction is a **court process** — Colorado calls it forcible entry and detainer (FED). The steps and timelines below reflect current law, but this area has changed almost every legislative session since 2019, so always check the current statute before you rely on a number.

### Notice before filing

Under C.R.S. 13-40-104, before filing an eviction for nonpayment or a lease violation, the landlord generally must serve a written **[[demand for compliance or possession]]**:

| Situation | Notice period |
|---|---|
| Nonpayment of rent (residential) | **10 days** to pay or move |
| Violation of a lease term (residential) | **10 days** to cure or move |
| "Exempt" residential agreement (landlord owns 5 or fewer single-family rental homes and the lease says so) | 5 days |
| Nonresidential or employer-provided housing | 3 days |

A lease can't waive the notice. "Substantial violations" (such as certain violent or drug-related acts) follow a separate, shorter-notice track.

### No self-help

It is **unlawful** for a landlord to remove or lock out a tenant without court process — changing the locks, removing doors or windows, or willfully cutting off heat, water, electricity or other essential services (C.R.S. 38-12-510). The tenant can recover actual damages plus the greater of three months' rent or $5,000, and attorney fees.

### "For cause" eviction

A 2024 law (HB24-1098, C.R.S. 38-12-1301 et seq.) generally requires a landlord to have **[[For-cause eviction|cause]]** to evict a covered residential tenant **or to refuse to renew** the lease once the tenant has lived in the unit for **12 months**. Cause includes nonpayment, substantial or repeated lease violations, nuisance and damage. Certain **[[No-fault eviction|no-fault]]** reasons — such as demolition or conversion, substantial renovation, the landlord or a family member moving in, withdrawing the unit to sell it, or the tenant refusing a reasonable new lease — allow non-renewal with longer written notice (generally 90 days). Exemptions include short-term rentals, employer-provided housing, and certain owner-occupied single-family homes, duplexes and triplexes. The details have been amended since, so treat this as a principle: **in Colorado, a landlord usually can't simply decline to renew a long-term tenant without a reason.**

> **Exam tip:** If an answer has the landlord changing the locks, shutting off utilities, or moving the tenant's belongings without a court order, it's wrong — no matter how much rent is owed.

## Where the broker fits

- Use a written **[[Management agreement|property management agreement]]** and the Commission-approved listing forms for leasing (Exclusive Right to Lease, Exclusive Tenant) where appropriate.
- Lead-based paint disclosure applies to pre-1978 rentals.
- Fair housing laws, including Colorado's **[[source of income]]** protection, apply to leasing (see the fair housing lesson).

lessons.title: Water rights, wells, minerals and Colorado taxes
lessons.body:
## Colorado water law in one sentence

Colorado follows the **[[prior appropriation]]** doctrine: "first in time, first in right." The person who first put water to a beneficial use has the **[[Senior water right|senior]]** right; later users are **[[Junior water right|junior]]** and must stop diverting when there isn't enough water for seniors (a "call" on the river). Owning land next to a stream does **not** by itself give you the right to use its water — that's the riparian system used in many eastern states, and Colorado rejects it.

## Water rights are separate property

A Colorado [[water right]] is a property right in its own right. It can be sold with the land or **severed and sold separately**.

- Water rights are conveyed with **the same formalities as real estate** (C.R.S. 38-30-102) — usually by a **[[deed]]** recorded with the county clerk and recorder.
- Shares in a **[[Mutual ditch company|mutual ditch company]]** are the exception: they are personal property (stock) and transfer by stock assignment and a new certificate from the company.
- If a deed is silent, a water right may or may not pass as an appurtenance depending on intent — a lawsuit waiting to happen. Good practice is to **list water rights expressly** in the contract and the deed.
- The residential contract has a section listing water rights, well rights, water stock and other water included in the sale.

## Source of Water

Buyers must learn where their drinking water comes from. The contract requires the buyer to acknowledge receiving either the **[[Seller's Property Disclosure]]** or the **[[Source of Water Addendum]]** disclosing the potable water source (water provider, well, cistern, etc.), and — if there's a well — a copy of the current well permit. The contract warns in capital letters that some water providers rely to varying degrees on nonrenewable groundwater and suggests buyers contact the provider about long-term supply.

## Wells and the change-of-ownership filing

Most household wells in Colorado operate under a permit from the State Engineer (Division of Water Resources). Common **[[exempt well]]** types:

- **[[Household-use-only well|Household use only]]** — usually on smaller parcels; indoor use in one home, no outside watering.
- **[[Domestic and livestock well|Domestic and livestock]]** — usually on 35+ acres; up to three homes, up to one acre of lawn and garden, and livestock watering.

A buyer must stay within the permit's limits; a seller's lawn sprinklers on a household-use-only well are a red flag.

**[[Change in owner name form|Change in ownership]]** (C.R.S. 38-30-102, updated 2023):

- On the sale of residential property with a small-capacity or domestic exempt well used for household purposes, the **buyer** must complete the Division of Water Resources' **[[Change in owner name form|change in owner name form]]** (or a registration form if the well was never registered).
- The **[[Closing company|closing service provider]]** (title company) submits the form to the Division **within 60 days after closing**. If there is no closing company, the buyer files it within 60 days and pays the fee.
- The Commission's contract has the buyer complete the form at or before closing so the closing company can file it.

> **Exam tip:** The well filing is the **buyer's** form, filed through the **[[closing company]]** after closing. The seller doesn't file it, and it doesn't go to the county assessor.

## Augmentation

Pumping a well that draws on groundwater connected to a stream takes water that senior surface users are entitled to. A **[[Non-exempt well|non-exempt]]** well (for example, for irrigation or a multi-home subdivision system) generally needs an **[[augmentation plan]]** approved by the **[[Water court|water court]]**, which replaces those depletions — the right amount, at the right time and place — often by buying senior water or using a membership in a water district's augmentation program. Buyers of properties that rely on augmentation need to confirm the plan or membership transfers and is current.

## Mineral rights severance

Just as water can be severed from land, so can minerals. A prior owner may have kept or sold the **[[mineral rights]]**, creating a *split estate*. The surface buyer then owns the land but not what lies beneath, and the mineral owner generally has a right to reasonable use of the surface to develop the minerals. Severed mineral interests show up in the title commitment's exceptions; brokers should point buyers to the title commitment and to legal counsel rather than give opinions on mineral title.

## Colorado property tax mechanics

The Colorado Division of Property Taxation describes the calculation in three steps:

1. The county assessor sets the **[[actual value]]** (market-based value). Real property is revalued every **odd-numbered year**, based on its classification and use as of **January 1**.
2. **Actual value × [[assessment rate]] = [[assessed value]].** The legislature sets the assessment rates, and they've changed several times recently — learn the formula, not the current percentage.
3. **Assessed value × [[mill levy]] = tax.** A mill is one-thousandth of a dollar, so divide mills by 1,000. Each taxing authority (county, school district, city, special districts) sets its own levy every year, and the levies are added together.

Example (made-up rates): actual value $400,000 × 6.5% = $26,000 assessed; $26,000 × 90 mills (0.090) = **$2,340** tax.

Taxes are **[[paid in arrears]]** — due January 1 of the following year, payable in full by the end of April or in halves by the end of February and June 15. A property owner who disagrees with the value protests to the **[[assessor]]** first, then the **[[County board of equalization|county board of equalization]]**, then the Board of Assessment Appeals, district court or arbitration.

## Documentary fee and transfer declaration

- **[[Documentary fee]]:** one cent per $100 of consideration (a major fraction of $100 counts as $100), with no fee when consideration is $500 or less; collected by the clerk and recorder at recording.
- **[[Real property transfer declaration]] (TD-1000):** filed with the deed to report the sale price to the assessor; confidential.

## Special and metropolitan district disclosures

Much new Colorado housing sits in a **[[special taxing district]]**, often a **[[metropolitan district]]** that borrowed to build roads, water and sewer, and repays that debt through extra mill levies.

- Every residential sales contract must contain a **bold disclosure** that special taxing districts may carry general obligation debt and that owners may face **higher mill levies** if the district can't pay it otherwise; buyers should investigate, for example through the county treasurer's certificate of taxes due (C.R.S. 38-35.7-101). The **seller** has the duty, and a buyer who doesn't get it can sue for damages.
- Since 2024, a seller of residential property in a metropolitan district organized on or after January 1, 2000 must give the buyer the **district's official website**, on the Seller's Property Disclosure or a document delivered with it (C.R.S. 38-35.7-111). The contract has a blank for that website.

## Colorado nonresident withholding

When the seller is a **[[Colorado nonresident withholding|nonresident]]** (an individual whose address is outside Colorado, or a foreign corporation without a permanent place of business in Colorado), the closing or title company must withhold the **lesser of 2% of the sales price or the seller's net proceeds** and send it to the Colorado Department of Revenue (C.R.S. 39-22-604.5). Key exceptions:

- No withholding when the sales price is **$100,000 or less**.
- None when the seller signs an affirmation that they are a Colorado resident, the property was their **[[Principal residence|principal residence]]**, or no Colorado tax will be due on the gain.
- None on foreclosure transfers or deeds in lieu to the lender.

The withholding is a prepayment of the seller's Colorado income tax, not an extra tax.

## FIRPTA note

Separately, under the federal **[[FIRPTA]]** law, when the seller is a **[[Foreign person|foreign person]]**, the buyer is generally required to withhold a percentage of the amount realized and send it to the IRS, subject to exemptions (for example, some lower-priced homes the buyer will live in). In practice the closing company handles it. Don't mix them up: Colorado withholding turns on **Colorado residency**; FIRPTA turns on **foreign status**. A Texas resident who is a U.S. citizen may face Colorado withholding but not FIRPTA.

lessons.title: Colorado fair housing, foreclosure and the Foreclosure Protection Act
lessons.body:
## The [[Colorado Fair Housing Act]]

Colorado's housing discrimination law (C.R.S. 24-34-501 et seq.) covers everything the federal Fair Housing Act does and more. It's enforced by the **[[Colorado Civil Rights Division]]** (CCRD) and the Colorado Civil Rights Commission.

### Protected classes

| Federal Fair Housing Act | Colorado adds |
|---|---|
| Race | Creed |
| Color | Sexual orientation |
| Religion | Gender identity |
| Sex | Gender expression |
| National origin | Marital status |
| Familial status | Ancestry |
| Disability (handicap) | Veteran or military status (2022) |
| | [[Source of income]] (2021) |

So the Colorado list in the main housing section is: disability, race, creed, color, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, marital status, familial status, veteran or military status, religion, national origin and ancestry — plus separate provisions covering **[[source of income]]**.

### Source of income

A landlord can't refuse to rent to someone, or set different terms, because of a **lawful, verifiable** source of money — wages, Social Security, child support, or government or private rental assistance such as housing vouchers. Landlords with **three or fewer** rental units are exempt from the source-of-income provisions, and a landlord may still check credit as long as it checks **every** prospective tenant. A separate small-landlord rule lets an owner of no more than five single-family rentals (and no more than five rental units in all) decline federal housing choice vouchers for those homes.

### Enforcement

- A person who believes they faced housing discrimination may file a charge with the **[[CCRD]] within one year** of the discriminatory act.
- The CCRD investigates; cases can go to hearing or court, and a private lawsuit is possible within two years.
- For a broker, a fair housing violation is also grounds for license discipline.

> **Exam tip:** Exam questions like to ask which class is protected in Colorado but **not** under federal law. Marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, creed, ancestry, veteran/military status and source of income are Colorado additions. Familial status and disability are protected by both.

## Colorado foreclosure: the public trustee system

In Colorado, a home loan is secured by a **[[deed of trust]]** — but unlike most deed-of-trust states, the trustee isn't a private company. The trustee is a government official, the county **[[public trustee]]**, and almost all foreclosures are non-judicial sales conducted by that office under C.R.S. Title 38, Article 38. (Some foreclosures go through the courts and a sheriff's sale instead.)

### The basic sequence

1. **[[Default]].** The borrower falls behind.
2. **[[Notice of Election and Demand]].** The lender's attorney files the foreclosure papers with the public trustee, who records the **[[notice of election and demand]]** with the county clerk and recorder. This starts the clock.
3. **[[Rule 120 hearing|Court order authorizing sale]].** A short court proceeding (commonly called a "Rule 120" hearing) confirms the lender may proceed.
4. **Notices and publication.** The public trustee mails notices to the owner and others with recorded interests and publishes a combined notice of the sale and the rights to cure and redeem for several weeks.
5. **Sale.** For non-agricultural property, the sale date is set **110 to 125 days** after the notice of election and demand is recorded (215 to 230 days for agricultural property). The lender usually bids its debt, and the highest bidder gets a **[[certificate of purchase]]**.
6. **[[Redemption]] periods** for junior lienors, then the **[[Confirmation deed|public trustee's confirmation deed]]** to the holder of the certificate.

### Cure before the sale

The owner (and certain others, such as junior lienholders and guarantors) can **[[cure]]** the default — pay the past-due amounts, fees and costs, not the whole loan — and stop the sale:

- File a **[[Notice of intent to cure|notice of intent to cure]]** with the public trustee **at least 15 calendar days before the sale**.
- Pay the cure amount **by noon on the day before the sale**.

### Redemption after the sale

Under current Colorado law, the **owner has no right to redeem after the sale**. Post-sale [[redemption]] belongs to **[[Junior lienor|junior lienors]]** (for example, a second mortgage lender) whose liens were recorded before the notice of election and demand. A junior lienor must file a notice of intent to redeem within **8 business days** after the sale, and the redemption periods run in order of lien priority. If nobody redeems, the certificate holder gets the deed.

> **Exam tip:** In Colorado the borrower's big window is **cure before the sale**, not redemption after. Don't pick an answer giving the homeowner months to redeem after a public trustee sale.

### Short sales

A **[[short sale]]** is a sale where the lender agrees to accept less than the full payoff and release its lien. The lender's approval is a condition of the deal. The Commission has an approved **[[Short Sale Addendum]]** to the Contract to Buy and Sell, and using it is part of what keeps a short sale outside the CFPA's equity-purchaser rules. Short sales may have tax and deficiency consequences for the seller, so brokers should recommend legal and tax advice.

## The [[Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act]] (CFPA)

The CFPA (C.R.S. 6-1-1101 et seq.) protects homeowners facing foreclosure from schemes that strip their equity or take their homes. It regulates two kinds of people:

### [[Foreclosure consultants]]

People who, for a fee, offer to stop or postpone a foreclosure, get forbearance or arrange a loan for a homeowner. They must use a written contract with specific terms, and they may **not**:

- collect any fee **until they've fully performed every promised service**,
- take a lien or wage assignment to secure their fee,
- acquire any interest in the homeowner's property, or
- get a power of attorney from the homeowner (with narrow exceptions).

The homeowner may cancel a foreclosure consultant contract **at any time** by written notice.

A **licensed real estate broker acting within the license** (for example, listing the home for sale) is **not** a foreclosure consultant. Attorneys acting for clients and lenders handling their own loans are also excluded.

### [[Equity purchasers]]

An equity purchaser is someone who buys a **[[residence in foreclosure]]** — the owner's **[[Principal residence|principal residence]]** with a home loan **at least 30 days delinquent or in default** — other than a buyer who will live there as their own home. Exclusions include buyers at the public trustee sale, deeds in lieu to the lender, transfers between relatives, and a **short sale using the Commission-approved short sale addendum** that complies with the Act's short sale section.

Equity purchase contracts must meet strict requirements, and the homeowner may **cancel until midnight of the third business day after signing, or noon on the day before the foreclosure sale, whichever comes first**. The purchaser must return the homeowner's documents within 10 days of a cancellation.

### What it means for brokers

- The Commission has a separate **[[Foreclosure Protection Act contract|CFPA version of the residential Contract to Buy and Sell]]** plus a **[[Seller Warning]]**, **[[Notice of Cancellation]]**, and **[[Homeowner Warning Notice]]**. The Division's worksheet points to the CFPA contract when an **investor** buyer is purchasing an **owner-occupied residence** from a seller the buyer knows is **30+ days delinquent**, and the deal isn't a short sale.
- If the seller will **lease back**, has a right to **repurchase**, or the buyer will **assume the seller's loan**, the CFPA contract can't be used — an **attorney** must draft the contract.
- If the seller's main language isn't English, the Homeowner Warning Notice must be translated — the broker should not translate it personally.
- A broker who buys a distressed homeowner's residence as an investor can be an equity purchaser. Violations can bring criminal penalties and consumer-protection damages.
- The Division's advice: unless you have real experience with distressed sales, involve your employing broker and legal counsel.

questions.stem: A title company is closing a sale in which Broker Ana represents the buyer. The title company prepares the closing statement. Under Colorado Commission rules, who is responsible for making sure the buyer receives an accurate, complete closing statement?
choices: Only the title company, because it prepared the statement
Ana, the broker with the brokerage relationship
No one, because the buyer signs to approve the statement
questions.explanation: Commission rules make the broker who has a brokerage relationship responsible for the proper closing and for ensuring the consumer receives an accurate, complete, detailed closing statement signed by the broker. Using a title company delegates the work, not the responsibility.

questions.stem: A broker cannot attend a closing because of a family emergency. What does Colorado's closing rule allow?
choices: A firm-designated broker may review and attend in her place, sharing responsibility
The broker may let the title company close alone, with no further broker involvement
The closing must be postponed until the broker can attend and sign the statement in person
The broker's unlicensed assistant may attend the closing and sign the closing statement
questions.explanation: The broker must attend or be reasonably available; a firm-designated substitute broker may attend instead and then assumes joint responsibility for the statement's accuracy, completeness and delivery.

questions.stem: Who signs the Commission-approved Closing Instructions form?
choices: The listing broker and the buyer's broker
The buyer's lender, the seller and the closing company
The buyer, the seller and the closing company
questions.explanation: Closing Instructions engage the closing company for the parties, so the buyer, seller and closing company sign. Brokers are not parties to the instructions.

questions.stem: Under Colorado's good funds law, which payment may a closing company generally disburse against immediately?
choices: A buyer's personal check for the down payment
A post-dated check from the seller
A wire transfer that has been received
A promise from the lender to wire funds tomorrow
questions.explanation: Disbursement may occur only after funds are received and available for immediate withdrawal; wires and cashier's, certified or teller's checks qualify. Personal checks and promised funds do not.

questions.stem: A home sells for $512,000. What is the Colorado documentary fee?
questions.explanation: The fee is one cent per $100 of consideration: $512,000 / 100 = 5,120 x $0.01 = $51.20.

questions.stem: Under the Colorado Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Residential), if neither title box is checked, who selects the title company and pays for the owner's title insurance policy?
choices: The buyer and seller split it equally
questions.explanation: The contract defaults to the seller-selects option, under which the seller selects the title company and pays for the owner's policy. Many other states use buyer-paid owner's policies, which makes this a common trap.

questions.stem: Colorado property taxes for 2026 become due on which date?
questions.explanation: Colorado taxes are due January 1 of the year after they are levied, so they are paid in arrears. That's why the seller is usually debited for the current-year taxes at closing.

questions.stem: Closing is in July. Current-year property taxes have not been paid. How are the seller's share of the taxes shown on the closing statement?
questions.explanation: Because taxes are paid in arrears, the buyer will pay the whole year's bill later. The seller owes the buyer for the seller's days of ownership, so it is a seller debit and a buyer credit.

questions.stem: Last year's taxes were $3,650. Closing is June 15 in a 365-day year; the buyer owns the day of closing and current taxes are unpaid. Using the Colorado contract's default basis, what is the tax proration?
questions.explanation: Daily rate $3,650 / 365 = $10. Seller's days are January 1 through June 14 = 165 days, so 165 x $10 = $1,650, debited to the seller and credited to the buyer because taxes are paid in arrears.

questions.stem: Unless the parties agree otherwise, the Colorado residential contract prorates general real estate taxes based on:
choices: The prior calendar year's taxes, using the latest mill levy and valuation
An estimate of the current year's taxes supplied by the listing broker
The average of the last three years of taxes shown by the county treasurer
The current year's taxes, re-prorated once the actual tax bill is issued
questions.explanation: The default basis is the taxes for the calendar year immediately before closing, using the most recent mill levy and assessed valuation. Prorations are final unless the parties agree otherwise in writing.

questions.stem: A seller collected June rent of $1,800 on June 1. Closing is June 15 (30-day month) and the buyer owns the day of closing. What is the rent proration?
questions.explanation: Daily rent is $1,800 / 30 = $60. The buyer owns June 15 through June 30, 16 days: 16 x $60 = $960. The seller collected rent belonging to the buyer, so the seller is debited.

questions.stem: How are tenants' security deposits typically handled on the closing statement when a rental property is sold with leases assigned to the buyer?
choices: Prorated between buyer and seller by the days left on each lease
Credit seller and debit buyer the full amount of the deposits
Debit seller and credit buyer the full amount of the deposits
Left off the statement and refunded directly to the tenants
questions.explanation: Security deposits belong to the tenants and are transferred in full, not prorated: the seller is debited and the buyer credited. The contract also requires the seller to notify tenants in writing.

questions.stem: The seller prepaid $300 in HOA dues for June. Closing is June 15 (30-day month); the buyer owns the day of closing. How is this shown?
questions.explanation: The daily amount is $10, and the buyer gets 16 days (June 15 to 30), so $160. The seller paid in advance for days the buyer will enjoy, so the seller is credited and the buyer debited.

questions.stem: On a closing statement, the buyer's earnest money deposit is shown as:
questions.explanation: Earnest money has already been paid toward the price, so the buyer is credited. It is not a separate seller entry because the seller is credited with the full purchase price.

questions.stem: Which item would appear ONLY on the seller's side of a closing statement?
choices: Proration of HOA dues the seller prepaid
Payoff of the seller's existing loan
questions.explanation: Loan payoffs go to a third party (the seller's lender), so they appear only as a seller debit. The price and prorations are between buyer and seller, so they appear on both sides.

questions.stem: A seller who lives in Arizona sells a $350,000 Colorado rental property. Absent an exemption, what must the closing company do under Colorado law?
choices: Withhold 15% of the amount realized and remit it to the IRS under FIRPTA
Withhold nothing, because the seller is a U.S. citizen and not a foreign person
Withhold the lesser of 2% of the price or net proceeds for the Colorado Department of Revenue
Collect a 2% state transfer tax from the buyer and pay it to the county clerk and recorder
questions.explanation: Colorado requires the closing company to withhold the lesser of 2% of the price or net proceeds from nonresident sellers when the price exceeds $100,000, unless an exemption applies. FIRPTA (federal) applies to foreign persons, not to U.S. residents of other states.

questions.stem: Under Colorado law, the maximum security deposit a residential landlord may require is:
questions.explanation: A 2023 statute (C.R.S. 38-12-102.5) caps residential security deposits at two months' rent.

questions.stem: A residential lease is silent about the deposit return period. The tenant moves out and the landlord accepts the premises on March 31. By when must the landlord return the deposit or provide a written statement of deductions?
questions.explanation: Since January 1, 2026, Colorado gives the landlord 30 days after the lease ends or the premises are surrendered, whichever is later; a lease can extend that to no more than 60 days. Since this lease is silent, 30 days applies.

questions.stem: A landlord willfully keeps a tenant's deposit without cause. Under Colorado law, the landlord can be liable for:
choices: Only the amount withheld, with each side paying its own attorney fees
Twice the amount withheld, plus court costs but not attorney fees
A fixed $500 statutory penalty in addition to the deposit itself
Treble the amount wrongfully withheld, plus attorney fees and costs
questions.explanation: Wrongful retention exposes the landlord to treble the amount wrongfully withheld plus reasonable attorney fees and court costs, after the tenant gives at least 7 days' notice before suing.

questions.stem: A tenant falls behind on rent in a typical Colorado apartment. Before filing an eviction for nonpayment, the landlord generally must give a written demand allowing the tenant how long to pay or move?
questions.explanation: C.R.S. 13-40-104 generally requires 10 days' written notice for residential nonpayment. Shorter periods apply only to exempt small-landlord agreements (5 days) and nonresidential or employer-provided housing (3 days).

questions.stem: Which of the following is a protected class under the Colorado Fair Housing Act but NOT under the federal Fair Housing Act?
questions.explanation: Colorado adds marital status, creed, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, ancestry, veteran or military status, and source of income. Familial status, disability and national origin are protected by both.

questions.stem: A Colorado landlord refuses to rent to an applicant because her rent would be paid partly with a housing voucher. This most likely violates Colorado law based on:
questions.explanation: Colorado protects lawful, verifiable sources of income, including rental assistance, though some small landlords are exempt from parts of these provisions.

questions.stem: Colorado water law is based on which doctrine?
choices: Riparian rights (reasonable use by streamside owners)
Prior appropriation (first in time, first in right)
questions.explanation: Colorado uses prior appropriation: the earliest beneficial user holds the senior right. Owning land along a stream does not by itself give a right to use the water.

questions.stem: A buyer is purchasing a home with a domestic exempt well used for household purposes. Under Colorado law, how is the well's change of ownership handled?
choices: The seller files a well transfer notice with the county assessor before the home is listed
The listing broker files the change form with the water court at the closing table
The buyer completes the form; the closing company files it with the state within 60 days
No filing is needed, because exempt wells are outside the State Engineer's permit system
questions.explanation: The buyer completes the Division of Water Resources change in owner name form; the closing service provider submits it to the Division within 60 days after closing (or the buyer files it if there is no closing company).

questions.stem: A county assessor values a home at $400,000. If the assessment rate is 6.5% and the total mill levy is 90 mills, what is the annual property tax?
In a Colorado public trustee foreclosure, by when must the homeowner file a notice of intent to cure?
choices: At least 15 calendar days before the sale
Within 8 business days after the sale
At any time up to the moment of the sale
By noon on the day of the foreclosure sale
questions.explanation: The owner must file a notice of intent to cure no later than 15 calendar days before the sale and pay the cure amount by noon the day before the sale. Colorado owners have no post-sale redemption right.

questions.stem: An investor wants to buy the principal residence of an owner who is 60 days behind on the mortgage. It is not a short sale. Under the Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act, how long does the homeowner have to cancel the contract with this equity purchaser?
choices: Until the closing date, as long as the investor has not yet recorded the deed
For five calendar days after signing, by written notice delivered to the investor
There is no right to cancel once the homeowner has signed a compliant contract
Until midnight of the 3rd business day after signing, or noon the day before the sale if earlier
questions.explanation: C.R.S. 6-1-1113 lets the homeowner cancel an equity purchase contract until midnight of the third business day after signing, or noon on the day before the foreclosure sale, whichever comes first.

questions.stem: Match each closing item to the way it is entered on a Colorado closing statement.
left: Earnest money the buyer already paid
HOA dues the seller paid ahead, for the buyer's days
Unpaid current-year property taxes, for the seller's days
Rent the seller collected ahead, for the buyer's days
questions.explanation: Earnest money and a loan payoff involve an outsider, so they are single entries (buyer credit; seller debit). Prepaid HOA dues: the buyer reimburses the seller (buyer debit, seller credit). Taxes paid in arrears and rent collected ahead both leave the seller owing the buyer (seller debit, buyer credit).

questions.stem: The seller filled the propane tank last month, and the contract prorates the fuel left in the tank, worth $420 at closing. How is it entered?
questions.explanation: The seller paid ahead for fuel the buyer will use, so the buyer reimburses the seller: a double entry, buyer debit and seller credit. It moves between the parties, so it appears on both sides.

questions.stem: Which question tells you whether a closing item is a single entry or a double entry?
choices: Does money move between the buyer and the seller, or between one party and an outsider?
Is the item required by the lender?
Was the item paid in advance or in arrears?
questions.explanation: Items between the buyer and seller (price, prorations, concessions) are double entries; items between one party and an outsider (a lender, the county, a title company, a brokerage) are single entries. Advance versus arrears decides which way a proration goes, not whether it's double.

questions.stem: Closing is September 10 (not a leap year). Last year's taxes were $4,380, current-year taxes are unpaid, the year has 365 days and the buyer owns the day of closing. What is the tax entry?
questions.explanation: Daily rate $4,380 ÷ 365 = $12. The seller owned January 1 through September 9 = 252 days: 252 × $12 = $3,024. Colorado taxes are paid in arrears (the buyer will pay this year's bill), so the seller is debited and the buyer credited. $3,036 counts the closing day for the seller; $1,356 is the buyer's 113 days.

questions.stem: A seller collected September rent of $2,100 on September 1. Closing is September 10 in a 30-day month, and the buyer owns the day of closing. What is the rent entry?
questions.explanation: Daily rent $2,100 ÷ 30 = $70. The buyer owns September 10 through 30 = 21 days: 21 × $70 = $1,470. The seller already collected money that belongs to the buyer, so the seller is debited and the buyer credited. $630 is the seller's 9 days.

questions.stem: Which of these is entered as a seller debit and a buyer credit?
choices: Accrued interest on a loan the buyer assumes, when interest is paid in arrears
HOA dues the seller paid for the rest of the quarter
questions.explanation: Interest paid in arrears: the buyer's next payment will cover days the seller owned, so the seller pays the buyer for them (seller debit, buyer credit). Prepaid HOA dues go the other way, the price is a buyer debit and seller credit, and the new loan is a buyer credit only.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a proration in order.
choices: Count the days that belong to the party being charged
Multiply the rate by the days
Decide who is debited and who is credited
questions.explanation: Rate, days, multiply, then post it: for example $3,650 ÷ 365 = $10 a day, 165 seller days, $1,650, debited to the seller and credited to the buyer for taxes paid in arrears.

questions.stem: A student enters the buyer's $12,000 earnest money as a seller debit. What's wrong?
choices: Earnest money is only a buyer credit; the seller is already credited with the full price
Earnest money should be a seller credit
Earnest money should be a buyer debit
Nothing; earnest money is a double entry
questions.explanation: The deposit is part of how the buyer pays the price, so it reduces what the buyer brings (buyer credit). The seller's side already shows the full price as a credit; debiting the seller would take the deposit away from them.

questions.stem: On a correct closing statement, the property tax proration appears as a $2,310 seller debit and a $2,130 buyer credit. What does that tell you?
choices: One of the amounts is wrong: a double entry has the same amount on both sides
Nothing; buyer and seller amounts can differ
The difference is the documentary fee
The difference goes to the broker
questions.explanation: A proration moves value between the parties, so it is the same amount on both sides. Different amounts mean a math or copying error (here, transposed digits).

cards.front: Who is responsible for the proper closing of a Colorado transaction when a title company closes?
cards.back: The broker with the brokerage relationship; using a closing company doesn't remove that responsibility.

cards.front: What must the consumer receive from the broker at closing?
cards.back: An accurate, complete and detailed closing statement signed by the broker.

cards.front: Broker can't attend closing — what then?
cards.back: A firm-designated broker may attend and shares (joint) responsibility for the statement's accuracy, completeness and delivery.

cards.front: Failing to give buyer and seller a closing statement violates which statute?
cards.back: C.R.S. 12-10-217(1)(j) — a ground for license discipline.

cards.front: Who signs the Commission's Closing Instructions?
cards.back: Buyer, seller and closing company. Brokers are not parties.
C.R.S. 38-35-125: no disbursement until funds are received and available for immediate withdrawal (wire, cashier's/certified/teller's check).
Closing statement: required by Colorado license law in every deal. Closing Disclosure: federal TRID form for most consumer mortgage loans.
One cent per $100 of consideration; none if consideration is $500 or less.
The county clerk and recorder, when the deed is recorded.
Real Property Transfer Declaration: reports sale price to the assessor; filed with the deed; confidential.
Race-notice: an unrecorded deed loses to a later buyer who records first without notice.

cards.front: Default title company selection in the CBS1 contract
cards.back: If neither box is checked, the seller selects the title company and pays for the owner's policy.
Deletes standard exceptions (e.g., unrecorded mechanics' liens, survey matters); contract says if it applies and who pays.

cards.front: When are Colorado property taxes due?
cards.back: January 1 of the year after they're levied — paid in arrears.
In full by the end of April, or in halves by the end of February and June 15.
Debit seller, credit buyer for the seller's share.
Taxes for the calendar year immediately before closing, with most recent mill levy and assessed valuation.

cards.front: Rent collected in advance by seller
cards.back: Debit seller, credit buyer for the buyer's days.
Transferred in full: debit seller, credit buyer. Not prorated.
Credit seller, debit buyer for the buyer's days.

cards.front: Are HOA reserves credited to the seller at closing?
cards.back: No, unless the governing documents say otherwise.

cards.front: Association status letter timing and cost
cards.back: Seller requests it at least 14 days before closing; seller pays the status letter fee.
Lesser of 2% of price or net proceeds; not when price is $100,000 or less, or with residency/principal-residence affirmation.

cards.front: Who needs a license to manage rentals for others in Colorado?
cards.back: Anyone leasing/renting for another for compensation — except a salaried on-site manager of an apartment/condo owner doing customary duties.
Separate accounts for rents and security deposits; deposit within 5 business days.
Two months' rent.
30 days after lease end or surrender (whichever is later), or longer if the lease says so — max 60 days.
Treble damages plus attorney fees and costs; tenant gives 7 days' notice before suing. Retaining 125%+ of actual damages is presumed unreasonable.
Respond within 24 hours of notice; begin remedial action within 24 hours (life/health/safety) or 96 hours (other uninhabitable conditions, with permission to enter).

cards.front: Residential notice for nonpayment or lease violation
cards.back: 10 days (5 for exempt small-landlord leases; 3 for nonresidential/employer housing).

cards.front: Can a landlord change locks or shut off utilities to evict?
cards.back: No — removal requires court process (C.R.S. 38-12-510).
Landlord generally needs cause to evict or refuse to renew a tenant who has lived there 12+ months; no-fault grounds need ~90 days' notice. Check current law.
Prior appropriation: first in time, first in right.
With the same formalities as real estate, usually by recorded deed; ditch company shares by stock assignment.
Buyer acknowledges Seller's Property Disclosure or Source of Water Addendum and, if a well, the current well permit.

cards.front: Who files the well change-in-ownership form?
cards.back: Buyer completes it; closing company submits it to Division of Water Resources within 60 days after closing.
Water-court-approved plan replacing a well's stream depletions so senior rights aren't injured.
Actual value x assessment rate = assessed value; assessed value x mill levy (mills/1,000) = tax.
Bold notice in every residential contract: districts may have debt and raise mill levies; seller's duty.
Seller gives buyer the district's official website (districts organized on/after Jan 1, 2000).
FIRPTA: foreign-person sellers (IRS). Colorado: nonresident sellers (Dept. of Revenue).
Creed, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, marital status, ancestry, veteran/military status, source of income.

cards.front: Deadline to file a housing charge with the CCRD
cards.back: Within one year of the alleged discriminatory act.
The county public trustee, under a deed of trust (non-judicial).
110–125 days after the notice of election and demand is recorded.
Notice of intent to cure 15+ calendar days before sale; pay by noon the day before sale.
Junior lienors only; owner has no post-sale redemption. Intent to redeem within 8 business days.
Protects homeowners in foreclosure from equity-stripping by foreclosure consultants and equity purchasers.

cards.front: Is a broker a foreclosure consultant?
cards.back: Not while acting within the license; but an investor-broker can be an equity purchaser.
Can't be collected until every promised service is fully performed.
Until midnight of the 3rd business day after signing or noon the day before the sale, whichever is first.

cards.front: When can't the CFPA contract be used?
cards.back: Seller leaseback, seller repurchase right, or buyer assuming the loan — an attorney must draft.

cards.front: Debit vs. credit on a closing statement, in plain words?
cards.back: Debit = the party owes it (buyer brings more / seller takes home less). Credit = in the party's favor (buyer brings less / seller takes home more).

cards.front: Single entry or double entry: how to tell?
cards.back: Between buyer and seller → double entry (same amount, both columns). Between one party and an outsider (lender, county, title company, broker) → single entry.

cards.front: Prorations: paid in advance vs. paid in arrears?
cards.back: Seller paid ahead (HOA dues, fuel) → buyer debit, seller credit. Paid in arrears (Colorado taxes, assumed-loan interest) → seller debit, buyer credit. Rent the seller collected ahead → seller debit, buyer credit.

cards.front: Propane left in the tank that the seller paid for?
cards.back: Buyer debit, seller credit (the buyer reimburses the seller).

glossary.definition: The title company or other settlement provider that prepares closing figures, collects and disburses funds, and records documents.
An itemized accounting of each party's debits and credits at closing; Colorado requires brokers to ensure parties receive an accurate one signed by the broker.
Commission-approved form engaging a closing company, signed by buyer, seller and the closing company.
Federal TRID form giving a borrower final loan terms and closing costs, for most consumer mortgage loans.
Funds received and available for immediate withdrawal, such as wires or cashier's checks, required before a Colorado closing provider disburses.
Colorado state fee of one cent per $100 of consideration, collected by the county clerk and recorder when a deed is recorded.
Form TD-1000 filed with a deed to report the sale price to the county assessor; confidential.
Recording system where a later buyer without notice of an earlier unrecorded interest wins by recording first; Colorado's system.
Title policy protecting the buyer's ownership; under the Colorado contract default, the seller pays for it.
Title coverage that removes standard exceptions such as unrecorded mechanics' liens and survey matters.
A charge to a party on a closing statement — something they owe.
An amount in a party's favor on a closing statement — something they receive or have already paid.
Dividing an expense or income between buyer and seller according to the time each owned the property.
Paid after the period it covers; Colorado property taxes are paid the year after they're levied.
Statement from an owners' association showing assessments and fees due on a unit, requested before closing.
A separate account holding money that belongs to others, such as rents, security deposits and earnest money.
Money a tenant pays to secure performance of a lease; in Colorado capped at two months' rent and returned within 30 days (up to 60 days by lease).
Implied promise in every Colorado residential lease that the unit is fit for human habitation; cannot be waived.
Written notice a landlord must give before filing eviction, usually 10 days for residential tenants in Colorado.
Colorado's water doctrine: the first person to put water to beneficial use has the senior right.
aliases: first in time, first in right

glossary.definition: A property right to divert and use a certain amount of water, which in Colorado can be conveyed separately from land.
Commission-approved addendum disclosing a property's potable water source.
A small household or domestic well permitted by the State Engineer outside the priority system, with limited uses.
Water-court-approved plan that replaces depletions from well pumping so senior water rights aren't injured.
Ownership of minerals beneath the surface, which can be severed from surface ownership.
The assessor's market-based value of property for property tax purposes.
Percentage set by law that converts actual value into assessed value.
Actual value times the assessment rate; the value the mill levy is applied to.
Property tax rate expressed in mills (thousandths of a dollar) per dollar of assessed value.
Local government unit, such as a metropolitan district, that can issue debt and levy property taxes for services or infrastructure.
Federal law requiring withholding at closing when the seller is a foreign person.
aliases: Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act

glossary.definition: Colorado's housing discrimination law (C.R.S. 24-34-501 et seq.), covering more protected classes than federal law.
State agency that investigates discrimination complaints, including housing.
Colorado protected class covering lawful, verifiable income, including rental assistance and vouchers.
Security instrument giving a trustee the power to sell the property if the loan isn't repaid; in Colorado it creates only a lien (C.R.S. 38-35-117), and the trustee is the county public trustee.
County official who acts as trustee under Colorado deeds of trust and conducts non-judicial foreclosure sales.
Document recorded by the public trustee that starts a Colorado foreclosure.
Paying past-due amounts and costs before the sale to stop a foreclosure and reinstate the loan.
Buying back property after a foreclosure sale; in Colorado available to junior lienors, not the owner.
Document given to the winning bidder at a public trustee sale, later exchanged for a confirmation deed.
Sale where the lender agrees to accept less than the loan balance and release its lien.
Law (C.R.S. 6-1-1101 et seq.) protecting homeowners in foreclosure from foreclosure consultants and equity purchasers.
Person who, for pay, offers to stop or delay a foreclosure or arrange relief for a homeowner; regulated by the CFPA.
Person who buys a residence in foreclosure, other than as their own residence; regulated by the CFPA.
Under the CFPA, an owner's principal residence with a home loan at least 30 days delinquent or in default.

The county official who records deeds, deeds of trust and other documents in the public records. In Colorado the clerk and recorder also collects the documentary fee and passes the transfer declaration to the assessor.

A certificate from the county treasurer showing any unpaid property taxes, special assessments and tax liens on a property. The title company usually orders one for closing, and the contract says who pays for it.

Colorado's rule that when a nonresident seller sells Colorado real estate for more than $100,000, the closing company withholds the lesser of 2% of the price or the seller's net proceeds and sends it to the Department of Revenue. It is a prepayment of the seller's Colorado income tax, with exceptions such as a former principal residence.

An annual ad valorem tax that local governments levy on real property based on its value; Colorado calculates it as actual value × assessment rate × mill levy. Colorado property taxes are paid in arrears, the year after they accrue.

Colorado's rule (HB24-1098) that a landlord generally needs a legal cause, such as nonpayment or serious lease violations, to evict a covered residential tenant or refuse to renew the lease after the tenant has lived there 12 months.

A non-renewal or eviction allowed under Colorado's for-cause law even though the tenant did nothing wrong, such as for demolition, substantial renovation, the owner or a family member moving in, or a sale. It generally requires longer written notice.
Under prior appropriation, a water right with an earlier appropriation date. Senior rights are filled first in a shortage, and juniors must stop diverting to satisfy them.
Under prior appropriation, a water right with a later appropriation date. When there isn't enough water, junior users must stop diverting so senior rights can be filled.

A company formed by water users to own and run a ditch or canal, with each shareholder entitled to a share of the water. In Colorado its shares are personal property and transfer by stock assignment, not by deed.
An exempt Colorado well permit that allows water for ordinary household uses inside a home only, with no lawn or garden watering or livestock. It is common on smaller parcels.
An exempt Colorado well permit, usually on 35 acres or more, that can serve up to three homes, water up to one acre of lawn and garden, and water livestock.

The Colorado Division of Water Resources form that records a new owner of a well. On a residential sale with an exempt household well, the buyer completes it and the closing company files it within 60 days after closing.

A well that needs more water or broader uses than an exempt permit allows, such as irrigation or a multi-home system. In Colorado it usually needs a water court-approved augmentation plan so it doesn't injure senior water rights.
A special district court that decides water-right matters in each of Colorado's seven water divisions, including approving new water rights, changes of water rights and augmentation plans.
The county official who sets the actual value of each property for property tax purposes. A Colorado owner who disagrees with a valuation protests to the assessor first.
The county body (usually the county commissioners) that hears a property owner's appeal after the assessor denies a valuation protest.
The home a person actually lives in as their main home. The term matters for Colorado nonresident withholding exemptions, the Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act and the federal home-sale exclusion.

For FIRPTA, a nonresident alien individual or a foreign corporation, partnership, trust or estate. When the seller is a foreign person, the buyer generally must withhold part of the amount realized for the IRS.

A limited Colorado court proceeding in a public trustee foreclosure that authorizes the sale. It mainly checks whether a default has probably occurred and whether the borrower is protected as a servicemember.
The deed the public trustee issues to the holder of the certificate of purchase after all redemption periods end without redemption. It transfers title to the foreclosed property.
A written notice a Colorado owner (or other eligible party) files with the public trustee at least 15 calendar days before a foreclosure sale to preserve the right to cure the default.
A lienholder whose lien is lower in priority than the one being foreclosed, such as a second mortgage lender. In Colorado, eligible junior lienors may redeem after a public trustee sale.

The Commission-approved addendum to the Contract to Buy and Sell used when the seller's lender must approve a sale for less than the payoff. Using it helps keep a short sale outside the CFPA's equity-purchaser rules.

A Commission-approved form attached to the Foreclosure Protection Act contract that warns the seller the buyer is not assuming the seller's loans or liens, so the seller remains liable for them and any deficiency. The seller reads and signs it.

A Commission-approved form attached to the Foreclosure Protection Act contract that tells the homeowner they may cancel without penalty and how to do it. Its deadline must match the contract's cancellation date.

A Commission-approved notice attached to the Foreclosure Protection Act contract warning the homeowner that the sale has serious legal consequences, including a right to cancel, and urging them to consult an attorney or housing counselor. It must be translated into the seller's main language if needed, but not by the broker.
